segments.say: Fourteen ways to get root. On supermarket fridge controllers.
segments.show: VulnCheck disclosed 14 flaws in Copeland (Dixell) XWEB EVO refrigeration supervisors, each reproduced to root in its lab (13 Nov).

segments.say: VulnCheck says two are already being exploited.
segments.show: CVE-2026-124014 and CVE-2026-124010 hit VulnCheck's sensors on 12 and 13 Nov, from opportunistic scanners. No threat actor named.

segments.say: Support ended in March. VulnCheck says the current firmware won't be fixed.
segments.show: Copeland declared XWEB EVO end of software support (no fixes after 16 Mar 2026), per VulnCheck. About 1,663 hosts show up on Shodan.
segments.card: End of support: no more fixes

segments.say: Take them off the internet. Put them behind a V P N.
segments.show: VulnCheck and Copeland: keep the controllers off the public internet, segment them behind a VPN, and plan a move to a supported platform.

Fourteen ways to get root. On supermarket fridge controllers. 🧊

What VulnCheck and CyberScoop reported (13 Nov):
→ VulnCheck found 14 flaws in Copeland (Dixell) XWEB EVO refrigeration supervisors; each reached root in its lab
→ Two are exploited: CVE-2026-124014 and CVE-2026-124010 hit VulnCheck's sensors on 12 and 13 Nov
→ Copeland declared XWEB EVO end of software support in March; VulnCheck says the flaws in current firmware won't be fixed

What to do: find every XWEB EVO you run, take it off the public internet, put it behind a VPN and plan the move to a supported platform.

cover.hook: Expedia confirms a breach. Hackers claim nearly a billion records.
cover.sub: Expedia says attackers got in through a third-party data platform. It hasn't confirmed the group's numbers.

slides.title: What Expedia confirmed
slides.body: Expedia told Skift attackers reached its systems through a compromised third-party data platform provider, in a supply chain attack that also hit other companies. It says the investigation is ongoing and its platforms remain safe to use.

slides.title: What the hackers claim
slides.body: n0n, an extortion group that appeared in mid-September, claims 830M+ loyalty records from 35 programs, 58M traveler profiles and 333M+ account and credential records. Expedia hasn't confirmed these figures.

slides.label: traveler records claimed by n0n (unverified)
slides.note: Security Affairs, 14 Nov. n0n's leak site claims 224 attacks since September.

slides.title: The way in
slides.body: Wiz and Sentra say the attackers used a stolen vendor key from Qubole, a Google Cloud partner, which gave them a trusted path into Expedia's big data platform.

slides.title: Do this week
items: Change your Expedia password from a trusted device
Expect phishing that quotes your bookings or points
List vendors with standing keys to your data platform

items.question: Which vendor still holds a key to your data warehouse?

segments.say: Ransomware hit a cloud provider. Its customers went down with it.
segments.show: Belarusian cloud provider ActiveCloud, which serves Belarus and Russia, says hackers breached its systems and encrypted parts of its cloud (The Record, 13 Nov).

segments.say: Hosting, email and virtual machines were disrupted for days.
segments.show: E-Cloud, E-Cloud Protected and SmartMail were affected; the Smartpress news site was knocked offline. Key systems were back by Wednesday.

segments.say: Main services are back. Some customers may still struggle to restore their V Ms.
segments.show: ActiveCloud says it found no evidence customer data was stolen. The attackers and the way in haven't been named.

segments.say: Keep one backup your provider can't touch.
segments.show: Keep an offline or second-provider backup, and test restoring it.

What The Record reported (13 Nov):
→ ActiveCloud, a cloud provider serving Belarus and Russia, says hackers breached its systems and encrypted parts of its cloud infrastructure
→ E-Cloud, E-Cloud Protected and SmartMail were affected; the Smartpress news site went offline
→ Key systems were back by Wednesday; on Friday it said main services were restored, with some customers still having trouble restoring VMs

The lesson: your provider's outage is your outage. Keep one backup outside your provider and test restoring it.

cover.hook: Under 3 hours to privileged access. AI agents did the hacking.
cover.sub: The FBI's FLASH alert on ARTEX, an open-source AI attack framework in use since at least August.

slides.title: What the FBI says
slides.body: FLASH-20261113-001 (13 Nov) covers ARTEX, an open-source multi-agent pentest framework written in Go. Operators give it a goal in plain language; agents run the commands. Attacker setups mostly use Chinese models, led by DeepSeek Flash.

slides.title: No zero-days needed
slides.body: The alert cites no CVEs. The way in: SQL injection, missing API authentication, unsigned SAML assertions, hardcoded passwords and unrotated keys. Some intrusions reached privileged access in under three hours.

slides.label: directory objects mapped by ARTEX agents
slides.note: They also hunted for Windows hosts without endpoint protection and added credentials to existing apps (Cyber Security News, 14 Nov).

slides.title: The scale
slides.body: Reported campaigns: personal data on about 67,000 people in South Korea, and 2,250+ Microsoft 365 tenants targeted through ConnectWise Cloud Backup. The repo was pulled on 8 Oct; forks remain, with 1,600+ exposed consoles found in early November.

slides.title: FBI's advice
items: Take Kudu/SCM, hypervisor and backup consoles off the internet
Cut app consent permissions to the minimum
Scan repos for secrets, rotate, and watch for odd LLM API traffic

items.question: Would your SOC notice 1,500 commands an hour from one account?

x_thread:
FBI FLASH on ARTEX, an open-source AI agent attack framework: some intrusions reached privileged access in under 3 hours, using known weaknesses, not zero-days. Attacker setups mostly run DeepSeek Flash.

The week's lessons 🧵 #AISecurity #CyberSecurity

1/ The alert: FLASH-20261113-001, 13 Nov. ARTEX is an open-source multi-agent pentest framework in Go. Operators type a goal; agents plan and run the commands. Used by a variety of actors since at least August, across ten sectors.

2/ The way in was old: SQL injection, missing API auth, unsigned SAML assertions, hardcoded passwords, unrotated keys. Inside, agents mapped 110,000+ directory objects, hunted for hosts without EDR and added credentials to existing apps.

3/ Same week, same pattern: Unit 42 says attackers ran 25 operations against 19+ orgs with the Cairn AI framework and GLM/DeepSeek models, with access or data taken at 10. Arctic Wolf tied AntiFox, built on ARTEX, to reads of AWS production secrets.
4/ The lesson: AI agents don't need new bugs. They work through the weak credentials and exposed consoles you already have, faster and around the clock.

5/ Do this week: inventory internet-facing apps; take Kudu/SCM, hypervisor and backup consoles off the internet; cut app consent rights; scan repos for secrets and rotate; alert on unexpected LLM API traffic.

6/ Question: would your SOC notice 1,500 commands an hour from one account?

Sources: Cyber Security News, SafeBreach via Security Boulevard, GBHackers (14 Nov); Unit 42 (12 Nov); The Hacker News (11 Nov).

segments.say: Myth: a confidential V M is safe from your cloud host.
segments.show: New research on AMD SEV-SNP, the tech behind many confidential VMs: two attacks let a malicious host read data inside them (The Hacker News, 13 Nov).
segments.card: Myth: the host can't see in

segments.say: Researchers read its memory in all one thousand lab tries.
segments.show: ETH Zurich's Mior attack (CVE-2026-0462) enabled debugging on a protected VM and read and wrote its memory in all 1,000 lab attempts on an EPYC 9135.

segments.say: A second attack, Skyfall, pulled a disk encryption key from a test V M.
segments.show: Skyfall (ETH Zurich and Google, CVE-2026-40671) recovered register values and a disk-encryption key on Zen 3 and Zen 4 EPYC. Both attacks need control of the hypervisor; no attacks in the wild reported.
segments.card: Skyfall: disk key leaked in lab

segments.say: Ask your provider if A M D's firmware fixes are in.
segments.show: Fixes ship as AMD firmware and microcode through server makers' BIOS updates (AMD-SB-3059, AMD-SB-3061). Renting confidential VMs? Ask your provider.

AMD SEV-SNP: new Mior (CVE-2026-0462) and Skyfall (CVE-2026-40671) attacks let a rogue cloud host read data inside confidential VMs in lab tests. Both need hypervisor control. Fixes come via firmware and BIOS updates.

#ConfidentialComputing #InfoSec
items.ig_caption:
Myth: a confidential VM is safe from your cloud host. 🔍

What The Hacker News reported (13 Nov):
→ Two new attacks on AMD SEV-SNP let a malicious cloud host read data inside confidential VMs
→ Mior (ETH Zurich, CVE-2026-0462) enabled debugging on a protected VM and read and wrote its memory in all 1,000 lab attempts
→ Skyfall (ETH Zurich and Google, CVE-2026-40671) recovered register values and a disk-encryption key from a test VM
→ Reality check: both need control of the hypervisor, Mior also needs the BIOS and a PCIe device; no attacks in the wild are reported
→ Fixes ship as AMD firmware and microcode through server makers' BIOS updates; some are targeted for November and December

What to do: if you run EPYC servers, get the BIOS updates from your server maker. If you rent confidential VMs, ask your provider when AMD's fixes are applied.
